To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the time course of processing letters in different scripts is similar, that visual and abstract letter representations are processed at different times, and that visual letter representation is influenced by orthography.

(1) visual form and abstract representations of letters are differentially processed at different stages of letter processing; (2) the time course of visual form processing is remarkably similar across alphabets; (3) the time course and neural correlates of letter processing are remarkably similar in Roman and Arabic scripts; and (4) the pattern of data is consistent with a hierarchical model of letter processing.
the time course of visual letter processing is remarkably similar in the Roman and Arabic scripts.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural basis of visual and abstract letter processing in two alphabets and its implications for the study of reading and orthographies.
the question of how the brain processes letters.
the neural mechanisms of visual and abstract letter processing and their role in the visual word recognition process.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the time course of processing in different scripts (e.g., Arabic, Roman) follow a similar trajectory from the visual features to the visual form of the letter, independent of abstract representations.

letter processing in different orthographies follows a similar time course and the same hierarchical organization, but with some differences in the relative importance of visual and abstract letter representations.
the visual form of letters is important for the initial stages of processing but is not the final determinant of the identity of letters in the alphabetic orthographies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the visual features of a letter are processed first and then the abstract form of the letter, and this sequence is the same in all alphabets.
the visual form of the letters is a key factor in the early stages of letter processing, but abstract representations are also activated in the later stages of processing.
the neural correlates of letter processing are similar across alphabets, but the visual features and the abstract representations are not.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the visual form of letters is a key factor in the early stages of letter processing, but that this effect is short-lived, and that abstract letter processing emerges later.
the time course of processing letters in the two alphabetic scripts is similar, but the visual features are not the same.

visual features are processed early in visual word recognition and are important for the initial processing of letter identity, whereas abstract letter representations emerge later and are more important for the integration of letters into words.
